summary:
Pulsars is a health monitoring system that lets astronauts understand and manage their own health during long missions, when communication with Earth is delayed or interrupted. It combines live sensor data (heart rate, body temperature, blood oxygen), symptom logging, guided checkups, and an AI health assistant that detects trends and asks follow-up questions. Earth-based doctors get their own dashboard with logs, sensor history, alerts, and AI-generated reports, and can send checkups, treatment instructions, and messages back.

Pulsars is more than a reactive measure. It checks vitals against NASA-based thresholds and each astronaut’s personal baseline, and it considers spacecraft conditions like oxygen and humidity before flagging an anomaly. This reduces false alarms and helps catch real problems early. It matters because on missions far from Earth, astronauts cannot rely on real-time medical support.
details:
Pulsars has two interfaces that share the same data:

  • Astronaut dashboard: Shows live heart rate, body temperature, and blood oxygen with trend lines and status labels. Astronauts log symptoms (type, severity from 1 to 5, optional notes) and complete scheduled checkups, such as sleep quality questionnaires and blood pressure checks, with step-by-step instructions.
  • Health assistant (AI): Explains the astronaut’s data, detects trends, and asks follow-up questions when a symptom is logged. It does not give medical advice.
  • Earth doctor dashboard: Gives doctors the symptom logs, sensor levels over time, threshold alerts, and AI-generated reports. Doctors can send new checkups, treatment instructions, and messages.

Context-aware interpretation

Vitals that are normal on Earth can differ in space, so Pulsars does not use Earth norms. Thresholds are based on NASA data and adjusted to each astronaut’s own median values. The system also reads spacecraft conditions such as oxygen levels and humidity. When a vital looks abnormal, it first tries to stabilize those environmental factors and checks whether the vitals return to normal, rather than immediately attributing the anomaly to the astronaut’s health. The database already keeps a running average of each astronaut’s own heart rate, temperature and oxygen, updated with every reading, which is the base for these personal baselines.


Benefits and intended impact

  • Autonomy: astronauts can act on their health without waiting for a reply from Earth.
  • Early detection: gradual changes are noticed before they become emergencies.
  • Doctor efficiency: Earth teams review organized reports.
  • Reach beyond space: the same design fits polar stations, ships, and remote clinics where patient and doctor are far apart.
  • Privacy: the assistant runs on a local model, so symptom text stays on the astronaut’s own computer and the tool keeps working without a connection.


Scalability

The system supports one astronaut or a full crew, each with their own profile, baselines, and history. It is sensor-agnostic, so new wearables can be added without redesigning the interface. It can work offline on the spacecraft and sync when the link to Earth is available, and doctors can create new checkup templates for different missions.

Tools and technologies

  • Frontend: React with TypeScript, built with Vite. Custom CSS with a dark theme, high-contrast cards, and clear status labels so data can be read quickly.
  • Backend: Node.js with Express, serving the astronaut and doctor dashboards.
  • Database: PostgreSQL, accessed through Prisma ORM for sensor readings, symptom logs, checkups, and user profiles.
  • AI: Google MedGemma 1.5, which powers the health assistant. It explains the astronaut’s data, detects trends, and asks follow-up questions about symptoms. It is instructed not to give medical advice.

Creativity

  • A friendly assistant character (Vela) makes health data approachable in a high-stress environment.
  • The context-aware logic treats the spacecraft as part of the patient’s health picture, which most monitoring tools do not.
  • The assistant is designed to explain and ask questions rather than diagnose, keeping doctors in charge of medical decisions.

Factors the team considered

  • Communication delay with Earth and the need for offline use.
  • Normal vitals changing in microgravity, which is why thresholds use NASA data and personal baselines.
  • Safety: the AI never gives medical advice and escalates to doctors.
  • Usability under stress: short checkups (3 to 5 minutes), clear severity scales, and a layout that fits on one screen without scrolling.
  • Privacy of health data and who can see it. Health text is processed by a local model.
